edition.deck: Overnight, Poland reported a Russian cruise missile among objects that violated its airspace; global markets fell sharply, while climate negotiations ran past their deadline.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritise the reported airspace incursion and market falls, then the stalled climate talks and strong investigations. The Danish security story is framed around what authorities allege, not as an established Russian-directed plot.

content.headline: Poland says Russian missile violated its airspace during Ukraine attack
content.shortHeadline: Poland reports Russian missile in its airspace
content.standfirst: Warsaw says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that entered Polish airspace during an attack on Ukraine. No one was hurt, and Poland calls the incursion a provocation; Moscow has not commented.

image.caption: CCTV footage shows an explosion after Poland reported a Russian missile in its airspace.

sources.originalTitle: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk

segments.body: Poland says a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile struck a rural area near Nowy Lipowiec early on Friday, one of three objects that violated its airspace. Officials report no injuries or damage. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the incident did not appear accidental; Russia has not commented.

segments.title: Allies respond
segments.body: Nato chief Mark Rutte condemned what he called grave violations and said Nato jets were scrambled. Poland says it will seek additional support. The incident occurred during Russian attacks on Ukraine and a military exercise involving western allies in southeastern Poland.

The incursion came amid deadly Russian strikes on Ukraine. The BBC reports at least eight people were killed in attacks on Kyiv and Lviv, with further deaths and injuries in Kryvyi Rih. Moldova also reported a drone briefly crossing its airspace.

content.headline: Global markets slump as AI sell-off sends tech shares lower
content.shortHeadline: AI-linked sell-off pushes global markets lower
content.standfirst: US indexes fell sharply on Friday as investors reassessed the scale and returns of AI investment. Anthropic shares slid on their second day of trading, and losses spread across Asian and European markets.

image.caption: Anthropic shares fell on the company's second day of trading, amid a wider technology sell-off.

sources.originalTitle: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
Flere amerikanske aktier falder markant op til weekend

segments.body: US markets fell sharply on Friday: the S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow 1.9% and the Nasdaq 5.3%. The S&P 500 and Dow entered correction territory, meaning they were at least 10% below a recent high. Anthropic shares fell 8.5%, giving back part of their first-day gains.

segments.title: Investors question AI spending
segments.body: The reports link the broader sell-off to concerns about whether vast spending on AI infrastructure will produce returns, alongside company-specific worries. The Guardian describes heavy losses across chipmakers and Asian markets; DR reports a Danish pension investment chief saw the week's declines as unusually large, while warning prices could fall further.

perspectives.body: The Guardian's market analysts point to a possible liquidity effect: investors buying Anthropic shares may be selling other technology stocks to raise cash. They also say the pressure has spread beyond a handful of major companies.

content.headline: COP31 talks run overtime as countries dispute fossil fuel language
content.shortHeadline: COP31 talks overrun amid dispute on fossil fuels
content.standfirst: Negotiators missed the climate summit's scheduled Friday finish, with countries divided over a draft agreement that omits fossil fuels. African ministers and civil society groups also say climate finance and justice remain unresolved.

image.caption: Activists stage a silent protest outside the COP31 plenary hall in Antalya.

sources.originalTitle: Cop31 talks go into overtime as debate rages over lack of fossil fuels in draft deal
’Ved siden af dig står der et menneske, hvor konsekvenserne er hverdag’: Klimapanel svarede på spørgsmål om COP31

segments.body: COP31 negotiations in Antalya continued beyond their scheduled Friday finish as nearly 200 countries struggled to agree on a final text. A shorter draft issued earlier in the week dropped references to fossil fuels that had appeared in an earlier version, prompting objections from countries seeking a commitment to move away from them.

segments.title: Finance and competing priorities
segments.body: African ministers said countries facing the worst impacts should not be left to pay for a crisis they did not cause, and called for resources to match declarations. The EU says it and member states provided €32.3bn in public climate finance in 2025 and mobilised €9.3bn in private finance. Negotiators also disagree over carbon capture and the draft's approach to adaptation.

A Danish climate researcher speaking to DR sees possible progress on renewable electricity, but says the draft's retreat from fossil-fuel language and lack of agreement on how to increase adaptation support point the other way. The final text remains unsettled.

perspectives.body: The DR panel's assessment is mixed: renewable power could be an area for practical progress, but it says countries have not agreed how to deliver the proposed increase in adaptation support for lower-income nations.

content.headline: Formerly fined bail firm accused of continuing to leave migrants in detention
content.shortHeadline: Bail firm faces fresh allegations over detained migrants
content.standfirst: A BBC investigation traces how companies linked to a firm fined $811m continued operating in the US immigration-bail business. Clients describe delayed releases, lost deposits and uncertainty; the current company denies wrongdoing.

image.caption: Mildred Juarez says she remained in immigration detention after friends sent bail money to Libre Immigration Services.

sources.originalTitle: They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop

segments.body: Mildred Juarez says friends sent $2,600 to Libre Immigration Services to secure her release from immigration detention in Texas, but she remained locked up for a month. The company says it connects clients with licensed bail agents; it says another firm ultimately declined to work with Juarez. She was released after her friends hired a different agent and says her deposit was not returned.

segments.title: A business re-formed
segments.body: The BBC reports that Libre Immigration Services was established by a buyer of assets from Libre by Nexus, whose owners and company were found liable in 2024 for predatory practices against clients and fined $811m. A judge later voided the asset sale but did not close the new firm. Its response is that it never held the client lists and it denies wrongdoing.

The investigation includes accounts from former employees and another client who says her friend's bail was not paid for a month after she transferred $10,000. The company says it needed to verify information before pledging the bond. A hearing on alleged violations of the court order has not been scheduled.

content.headline: Philippine pet owners seek answers after cremation remains found dumped
content.shortHeadline: Pet owners seek answers after remains found dumped
content.standfirst: Rescuers say they have found about 170 dead pets at 15 sites near Manila, and many owners fear animals they paid to have cremated were discarded instead. Criminal complaints have been filed, but the extent and cause of the dumping remain unclear.

image.caption: Revecca Calling says she wants to know whether her dog Olaf was properly cremated.

sources.originalTitle: Dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream

segments.body: Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run an animal rescue group, say they have uncovered 15 sites in Bulacan containing the remains of about 170 pets. Some owners recognised animals from videos and images. Many believe their pets were sent there after being entrusted to cremation businesses, leaving them unsure whether the ashes they received were genuine.

segments.title: What investigators allege
segments.body: The Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation filed criminal complaints against four people, including the owner of Ahjay Paws and people connected to another crematorium. The NBI says one business sent remains to the other after its planned cremation machine did not arrive, and that the second firm paid a third party to bury them. Investigators have not confirmed claims that the case involves a wider criminal syndicate.

Ahjay Paws' owner has denied responsibility, according to local media, and the BBC says it could not contact the business. Pet HPHT has called the allegations false. Owners are seeking answers and accountability; animal welfare advocates are offering legal help and calling for a nationwide audit of pet cremation businesses.

content.headline: Judge approves Bayer's $7.25bn Roundup cancer settlement
content.shortHeadline: Bayer's $7.25bn Roundup settlement gets judge's approval
content.standfirst: A Missouri judge approved a settlement fund for people with non-Hodgkin lymphoma who used Roundup, including some who may become ill in future. Bayer denies that the weedkiller causes cancer, and some lawyers had argued the proposed payouts were inadequate.

sources.originalTitle: Judge approves $7.25bn settlement for Roundup weedkiller cancer claims

segments.body: A Missouri judge has approved Bayer's $7.25bn settlement of US claims alleging its Roundup weedkiller caused non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The fund is intended for users already diagnosed and for people who develop the cancer in future. Payments are expected to range from $10,000 to $165,000, depending on factors including use and illness severity.

segments.title: A long-running dispute
segments.body: Bayer will pay into the fund annually for up to 21 years. Some lawyers objected that the amounts would be insufficient, but the judge said he did not want to delay payments to sick claimants. Bayer denies Roundup causes cancer; the settlement follows years of litigation and earlier payouts by the company.

content.headline: South Africa's ANC scrambles to form city coalitions after election losses
content.shortHeadline: ANC seeks city coalitions after South African election setback
content.standfirst: The governing ANC won the most votes nationally but lost ground in local elections and is negotiating to retain influence in major cities. Its reluctance to partner with the Democratic Alliance could reshape coalitions ahead of a 27 November deadline.

image.caption: The ANC won the most votes overall but lost control in many councils it had led after the previous local elections.

sources.originalTitle: ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback

segments.body: The African National Congress suffered its weakest local-election result since taking power in 1994. It won 31% of the vote, down from 46% in the previous local election, and led in only two of South Africa's eight cities. Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.

segments.title: Coalitions and service delivery
segments.body: The pro-business Democratic Alliance led in Johannesburg, Pretoria and Ekurhuleni, while the ANC appears reluctant to repeat its national power-sharing arrangement with the DA in local councils. The ANC is courting smaller parties, including ActionSA in Gauteng; unstable coalitions have previously disrupted basic services in several cities.

The election reflects mounting frustration over corruption and basic services, including electricity, water and rubbish collection. Analysts quoted by the BBC caution that even new coalitions may need years to address the problems facing municipalities, particularly Johannesburg.

content.headline: Nepal's new prime minister heads to India for high-stakes first visit
content.shortHeadline: Nepal's new leader visits India amid hopes for a reset
content.standfirst: Balendra Shah is due to meet Narendra Modi on Sunday, with trade, energy, air links and flood reconstruction expected on the agenda. Nepal's unresolved border dispute and its close ties with both India and China complicate the effort to reset relations.

image.caption: Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah is due to visit Delhi for talks with India's Narendra Modi.

sources.originalTitle: A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test

segments.body: Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah arrives in India on Sunday for his first bilateral visit since his party took power in March. Talks with Narendra Modi are expected to cover economic and energy cooperation, air routes and reconstruction after August's floods, which killed more than 1,450 people in Nepal.

segments.title: A difficult balance
segments.body: India is Nepal's largest trading partner and a key source of fuel and transit access, but trade is heavily weighted in India's favour and the neighbours have an unresolved territorial dispute. Nepal is also balancing relations with China: Shah sent a parliamentary delegation there earlier this month before travelling to India.

A former Indian ambassador sees a chance for more pragmatic ties, while a Nepali analyst quoted by the BBC warns that Shah and his advisers lack diplomatic experience. Nepal's government estimates flood reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, and securing concrete help would be a test of the visit.

content.headline: UK and EU agree new food, emissions and youth mobility deals
content.shortHeadline: UK and EU seal food, emissions and youth mobility deals
content.standfirst: The agreements ease many food-export checks, link emissions-trading systems and create reciprocal schemes for up to 100,000 young people each year. A dispute over student fees could still delay approval, while the government says the package could boost growth.

image.caption: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President António Costa at the summit's closing press conference.

sources.originalTitle: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit
What exactly is in the deal between the UK and the EU?
Burnham ready to cut tuition fees for EU students to avoid Brexit deal collapse
Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform

segments.body: At Friday's Brussels summit, the UK and EU agreed deals on food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility. The food agreement is intended to remove most checks on animal and plant products from 2028. The emissions systems are also due to be linked from 2028, while each side is to offer up to 100,000 young people opportunities to live, work, travel and study across the Channel.

segments.title: Student fees remain unresolved
segments.body: The EU says it will not approve the three agreements until the sides resolve how tuition fees for students from the other party will be treated. They have six months to negotiate. The UK has resisted lowering fees for EU students, while EU leaders say they are confident a solution can be found. The Guardian reports that Britain will align with EU rules in the food and emissions areas without voting rights.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that an EU statement outside the joint text makes approval of all three agreements conditional on a fees deal. Burnham says the agreements are done, but their implementation is not yet secure.

segments.title: Economic claims and political challenge
segments.body: The UK government says the package could add up to £17bn a year to the economy; opposition leaders dispute the deal's fairness and its claimed economic benefits. Burnham says the agreements are a step towards closer cooperation but that any further relationship will be considered later. Parliament is expected to receive implementing legislation next week.

content.headline: Blackpool's young jobseekers face a cycle of rejection and inexperience
content.shortHeadline: Blackpool's young jobseekers caught in an experience trap
content.standfirst: More than one in five 16- to 24-year-olds in Blackpool are out of work and education, the highest share in England. Young applicants describe fierce competition and recruitment barriers, while local support programmes try to connect them with training and jobs.

image.caption: Amy Butterworth describes a difficult search for work in Blackpool.

sources.originalTitle: ‘You can’t get experience if no one’s employing you’: the vicious circle facing Blackpool’s Neets
Rayner’s crackdown on zero-hours contracts faces being scaled back

segments.body: Blackpool has England's highest proportion of 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training: more than one in five, according to the report. Amy Butterworth, 19, says she has sent many applications but is repeatedly told she lacks experience. In one case, interview slots offered by a retailer were gone within minutes.

segments.title: Local obstacles and support
segments.body: The report describes scarce year-round work, with some employers receiving 200 applications for each vacancy. It also cites concerns about AI screening and postcode-based exclusions, and notes high school absence and exclusion rates. Blackpool's Platform youth hub says it has supported more than 2,350 young people into learning, training or work since 2022.

Butterworth found training to work in a bar through the hub and hopes to become a tattooist. Her experience comes amid a wider UK debate about how to reduce youth unemployment without making employers less willing to hire, including discussion of proposed changes to zero-hours contracts.

content.headline: Ministers weigh further changes to zero-hours contract reforms
content.shortHeadline: Zero-hours reforms may be softened over hiring concerns
content.standfirst: The government is still deciding how its proposed guaranteed-hours rights would apply, with ministers considering thresholds and possible exemptions. Supporters say the changes should curb insecurity; critics fear they could deter hiring, particularly of young people.

image.caption: Proposed changes to zero-hours contracts could affect employers' hiring decisions.

sources.originalTitle: Rayner’s crackdown on zero-hours contracts faces being scaled back

segments.body: Ministers are considering how far to extend a right for workers on zero-hours contracts to be offered guaranteed hours based on regular work. Possible rules include a threshold of eight to 20 hours a week, but options under discussion range as high as 48 hours. The government has not published its response to the consultation or set out a final policy.

segments.title: The trade-off
segments.body: Former minister Alan Milburn has urged caution, citing government estimates that the proposals could cost businesses between £350m and £2.9bn a year and research suggesting some employers may reduce permanent recruitment. Supporters of reform argue that zero-hours arrangements can leave workers bearing the risk of uncertain hours and pay. The government says it is considering consultation responses.

content.headline: Far-right activist jailed for slashing asylum seekers' dinghy in Channel
content.shortHeadline: Activist jailed for slashing Channel migrant boat
content.standfirst: Daniel Thomas received a 15-month sentence after admitting criminal damage to a dinghy being assisted by rescue crews. The judge said his actions disrupted lifesaving and border-force work; Thomas's defence described the incident as performative activism.

image.caption: Daniel Thomas, who was sentenced after admitting he slashed a dinghy that had carried asylum seekers.

sources.originalTitle: Far-right activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing dinghy in Channel

segments.body: Daniel Thomas, founder of the anti-migration group Patriot Platform, was sentenced to 15 months in prison after admitting he slashed a dinghy in the Channel. The judge said he had deliberately interfered with Border Force, coastguard and RNLI operations. Thomas livestreamed the incident as rescue crews approached the boat.

The RNLI said the people on board had been at sea for 36 hours, with concerns about their deteriorating health and the dinghy failing. Thomas's barrister called the case unique and said the damage was a spur-of-the-moment opportunity, not premeditated. Thomas had five previous convictions, the prosecution told the court.

content.headline: Forecasters warn of UK's coldest autumn night so far
content.shortHeadline: UK faces its coldest night of autumn so far
content.standfirst: Temperatures could fall to -9C in parts of Scotland, with sub-zero conditions farther south. A cold-health alert remains in force across several northern regions until Monday morning, and flooding is possible in parts of England.

image.caption: Snow in Tow Law, County Durham, earlier this week.

sources.originalTitle: Friday night will be ‘coldest of the autumn so far’, UK forecasters say

segments.body: The Met Office forecast the coldest night of the autumn so far on Friday, with lows of -8C to -9C possible in some Scottish glens and sub-zero temperatures farther south. A low of -8.4C had already been recorded at Tulloch Bridge in the Highlands overnight on Thursday.

A yellow cold-health alert is in force for north-west and north-east England and Yorkshire and the Humber until 9am on Monday. The UK Health Security Agency says such conditions may increase pressure on health services and risks for vulnerable people. Twelve flood alerts were also in place for England after wet weather.

content.headline: Measles losses in US renew warning over falling UK vaccination rates
content.shortHeadline: US measles status lost as UK vaccination rates fall
content.standfirst: The US has lost its measles-free status after a prolonged outbreak, while UK vaccination coverage has declined over the past decade. A House of Lords report warns of widening inequalities and calls for better services in communities at risk.

image.caption: Measles can cause serious illness, but vaccination can prevent it.

sources.originalTitle: Why the US has joined the UK on a warning list for a deadly disease

segments.body: The US, Bolivia and Mexico have lost verification that measles is no longer circulating endemically, following a sustained outbreak that began in early 2025, the Pan American Health Organization says. The US has reported more than 4,000 cases this year. The UK lost its measles-free status earlier this year.

segments.title: UK vaccination gap
segments.body: A House of Lords committee says pre-school vaccination rates in England have fallen for more than a decade and are below the World Health Organization standard. Coverage of the first MMR dose fell from almost 93% around 2013 to below 88% in 2025-26. The report links lower coverage to poverty and service pressures, and says inequalities between communities have widened.

Measles can cause serious complications and is highly contagious, but vaccination can prevent it. The report says changes to NHS services, pressure on GPs and reduced continuity of care have contributed to falling uptake. The UK and US figures in the report are not a prediction of where outbreaks will spread next.

content.headline: Teacher arrested after missing sentencing for assaults on schoolboys
content.shortHeadline: Teacher arrested after missing indecent-assault sentencing
content.standfirst: Sally-Anne Bowen was arrested in Hampshire after failing to attend court for sentencing over indecent assaults on two pupils in the 1980s. A new sentencing date is to be set; Bowen had denied the allegations at trial.

image.caption: Sally-Anne Bowen was convicted of seven counts of indecent assault and later arrested after missing sentencing.

sources.originalTitle: Police arrest teacher who missed sentencing after indecent assault conviction

segments.body: Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, was arrested in Hampshire on suspicion of failing to appear at Harrow Crown Court, where she was due to be sentenced after being convicted of seven counts of indecent assault. The court heard she had not been found at her home after a warrant was issued.

The Met said officers from a neighbouring force located and arrested Bowen at about 3pm on Friday. A new sentencing date will be set. The trial concerned sexual relationships with two pupils at a north London boys' school in the late 1980s; Bowen denied the allegations and called them a fabrication.

content.headline: Denmark expels Russian defence attaché after alleged plot against rapper
content.shortHeadline: Denmark expels Russian diplomat over alleged rapper plot
content.standfirst: The government says a Russian defence attaché must leave within seven days after investigators reported indications that people linked to the banned Loyal to Familia gang helped plan an attack on Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner. Russia denies involvement.

image.caption: Concert organiser Albina Serhiienko with Kyivstoner and his wife on the evening the performance was cancelled.

sources.originalTitle: Russisk diplomat bliver udvist af Danmark efter sag om attentatforsøg
Det ved vi om rapperen, som Rusland angiveligt ville have dræbt i Danmark
FSB har tidligere anklaget rapper for organisering af terrorforsøg
Albina havde arrangeret koncert med ukrainsk rapper - så blev hun kontaktet af PET

segments.body: Denmark has ordered Russia's defence attaché to leave within seven days, with Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen saying the move sends a signal. The government says it will also stop issuing non-essential visas to Russian citizens and proposes tougher penalties for crimes carried out on behalf of a foreign state.

segments.title: What authorities allege
segments.body: PET says there are indications that senior members of the banned gang Loyal to Familia helped plan an attempted killing of Kyivstoner, a Ukrainian-American rapper, during a September visit. Two Danish men with alleged gang links are suspected of being hired by Russia's FSB; they were arrested near the concert venue. Russia's embassy denies Russian involvement.

segments.title: The cancelled concert
segments.body: Concert organiser Albina Serhiienko says PET contacted her a week before the show and asked that the rapper be protected. The performance was cancelled shortly before doors opened, but she says police asked her not to tell guests why. She says she was shocked by the later arrest news and grateful to Danish police and PET.

perspectives.body: Serhiienko describes being instructed to keep the security reason from concertgoers while police monitored the venue. Her account gives a first-hand view of how the alleged threat affected the event.

content.headline: Hardi considers moving production from Denmark, putting hundreds of jobs at risk
content.shortHeadline: Hardi proposal puts hundreds of Danish jobs at risk
content.standfirst: The manufacturer of agricultural sprayers is considering moving production to France and Romania, leaving development and sales in Denmark. The proposal could affect some of its 334 Danish employees, but the company says no final decision has been made.

image.caption: Hardi employee Steen Svendsen could be among those affected if production moves abroad.

sources.originalTitle: Weekendhumøret forsvandt i Nørre Alslev: Stor virksomhed varsler mulig udflytning

segments.body: Hardi's French owner, Exel Industries, is considering moving production from Nørre Alslev to France and Romania, with development and sales remaining in Denmark. The company has 334 employees in Denmark; it is not yet clear how many jobs could go. Hardi's managing director says the plan is a proposal, not a final decision.

segments.title: Local impact
segments.body: Workers and residents told DR the plant is important to the town and wider area. A local union representative says many employees have worked there for years and that some families may have more than one person on the payroll. The company says the proposal reflects a downturn in the agricultural machinery market.

content.headline: Danish pension fund leads investor lawsuit over Zuckerberg's control of Meta
content.shortHeadline: PFA leads lawsuit over Zuckerberg's proposed Meta shares
content.standfirst: PFA Pension has been named a lead plaintiff in an investor case challenging a proposed Meta share class that would let Mark Zuckerberg sell shares while retaining voting control. Meta has paused the plan and says it will defend itself.

image.caption: Mark Zuckerberg and Meta's board are defendants in a lawsuit over a proposed share plan.

sources.originalTitle: Dansk pensionsgigant får hovedrolle i retssag om Zuckerbergs magt i Meta

segments.body: Danish pension fund PFA and California State Teachers' Retirement System have been named lead plaintiffs in a consolidated Delaware lawsuit against Meta and Mark Zuckerberg. Investors argue a proposed non-voting share class would let Zuckerberg sell shares without weakening his control of the company.

segments.title: Meta's response
segments.body: Meta has paused the share plan, according to a court filing. The company says it is acting in shareholders' interests and will strongly defend itself. It has previously said the arrangement would let Zuckerberg sell shares to fund philanthropic work; the investors argue it would entrench his control while leaving other shareholders with no equivalent benefit.

PFA says it holds Meta shares worth about DKK 5.5bn and calls the case important because similar structures could be used by other companies. The lawsuit is scheduled for trial in April next year; any judgment could be appealed.

content.headline: Two TV 2 executives leave after controversy over hidden-camera programme
content.shortHeadline: TV 2 leaders depart after hidden-camera show backlash
content.standfirst: TV 2's content director and programme director are leaving after criticism of Alle elsker Rasmus, a hidden-camera series that the broadcaster apologised for and removed. An internal review is still under way.

image.caption: TV 2's content director and programme director are leaving after the programme controversy.

sources.originalTitle: Indholdsdirektør og programdirektør stopper på TV 2

segments.body: TV 2 says content director Ulla Pors and programme director Dorthe Thirstrup are leaving after criticism of Alle elsker Rasmus. In the programme, comedian Rasmus Wallbridge was led to believe he was directing a film; TV 2 later apologised and removed the series from its platforms.

The broadcaster says a review of the programme and its production is continuing, but that it has already concluded the programme area needs new leadership to rebuild trust. Findings are expected to be presented to the board in the coming weeks. Thirstrup said she had made mistakes and apologised to Wallbridge.

content.headline: Man Utd’s manager costs near £100m as Berrada defends the club hierarchy
content.shortHeadline: Man Utd’s manager costs near £100m as Berrada defends the club
content.standfirst: A new filing puts Manchester United’s hiring and firing bill since 2013 at £95m, before further costs are added. Chief executive Omar Berrada has also defended the club’s summer recruitment amid supporter criticism.

image.caption: Mauricio Pochettino held his first Manchester United news conference.

sources.originalTitle: Cost of Man Utd hiring and firing managers nears £100m
Man Utd fan criticism has gone too far at times - Berrada

segments.body:
Manchester United say they owe US Soccer £7.5m in compensation for Mauricio Pochettino’s release from his USA deal. That takes the club’s manager hiring and firing costs since Sir Alex Ferguson retired to £95m, a figure expected to pass £100m once the cost of Pochettino’s staff and Michael Carrick’s dismissal are included.

The club borrowed another £10m on 16 November, three days after announcing Pochettino. Its filing also shows £240m owed on its rolling credit limit and £417m in outstanding transfer fees, including £181m due after a year.

segments.title: Criticism and recruitment
segments.body: Berrada said he understood supporters’ frustration at United sitting 18th, and accepted that some criticism was fair, but said some had “crossed a line”. He defended the club’s summer signings, while acknowledging that it could have added a defender if the right player and value had been available.

perspectives.body: Berrada says United are happy with their summer recruitment and will not spend simply to silence critics. Pochettino, meanwhile, said he wants to be involved in the main decisions about the squad.

content.headline: England’s revival faces its toughest test yet against New Zealand
content.shortHeadline: England’s revival faces a major test against New Zealand
content.standfirst: After scoring 20 tries in wins over Australia and Japan, England meet an All Blacks side stung by a first defeat by Wales in 73 years. The contest will test whether England’s improved depth and attacking form can stand up to elite opposition.

image.caption: England beat Japan 78-15 last weekend.

sources.originalTitle: Stacked England aim to pile on style and add to All Black misery

segments.body: England’s emphatic recent wins have restored some confidence after five straight defeats earlier in the year. Their attack has produced 20 tries against Australia and Japan, but New Zealand are a substantially sterner test: the All Blacks have lost four of their past seven matches and arrive after their historic defeat by Wales.

segments.title: Depth back in the picture
segments.body: England have regained several players from injury, including full-back George Furbank and prop Will Stuart, while the bench offers further options such as Marcus Smith and Henry Pollock. They are still without Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, Tom Curry and Alex Mitchell, but coach Steve Borthwick says the squad’s depth is back to a level last seen a year ago.

content.headline: Cricket Australia backs Cummins as captain amid renewed sandpaper claims
content.shortHeadline: Cricket Australia backs Cummins amid renewed sandpaper claims
content.standfirst: Cricket Australia will continue to support Pat Cummins as Test captain as new accounts reopen the 2018 ball-tampering dispute. Cummins denies knowing about the plan; fast bowler Josh Hazlewood says he would consider leaving if Cummins were forced out.

image.caption: Pat Cummins, who was named Australia captain in 2021.

sources.originalTitle: Cummins retains Cricket Australia support as captain

segments.body: Cricket Australia is backing Cummins to remain captain, a role he has held since 2021, despite renewed allegations over the 2018 Cape Town Test. Cameron Bancroft’s recent account supported earlier claims by Usman Khawaja that the whole team knew about the plan to tamper with the ball. Cummins has denied involvement or knowledge and called Khawaja’s claims “100% wrong”.

segments.title: Backing from a team-mate
segments.body: Hazlewood, who played in the Cape Town Test, said he would consider quitting the team if Cummins were made to stand down. Bancroft has also alleged that players and coaches celebrated when the ball-tampering succeeded; those claims remain contested.

perspectives.body: Hazlewood called the recent criticism a “pile on” and said he wanted to back Cummins. His comments underline that the dispute could affect the current team as well as revisiting the 2018 scandal.

content.headline: Alcaraz reaches ATP Finals semi-finals with perfect group record
content.shortHeadline: Alcaraz reaches ATP Finals semis despite injury concerns
content.standfirst: Carlos Alcaraz beat Flavio Cobolli in straight sets to complete the group stage without defeat, despite a hamstring problem. He next faces Ben Shelton, while Daniil Medvedev meets Alexander Zverev in the other semi-final.

image.caption: Carlos Alcaraz is seeking his first ATP Finals title.

sources.originalTitle: Alcaraz puts aside injury concerns to take apart Cobolli

segments.body:
Alcaraz, wearing strapping on his left leg after hurting his hamstring against Daniil Medvedev, beat Flavio Cobolli 6-4 6-1 in 65 minutes. He did not face a break point and hit 29 winners, extending his winning run to 12 matches.

The Spaniard said the immediate challenge was recovering physically for the next day’s semi-final against Ben Shelton. Alcaraz has never won the season-ending title.

content.headline: Kim takes three-shot LPGA lead after hole-in-one; Hull stays in contention
content.shortHeadline: Kim leads LPGA finale by three; Hull remains in the mix
content.standfirst: A-Lim Kim’s hole-in-one helped her shoot 64 and move to 15 under at the CME Group Tour Championship. Charley Hull is four strokes back after a bogey-free 67, with the tournament’s $4m top prize still in play.

image.caption: A-Lim Kim, whose only major title came at the 2020 US Women’s Open.

sources.originalTitle: Kim moves clear at LPGA finale after hole-in-one

segments.body:
Kim made a hole-in-one at the par-three 16th on her way to a seven-under 64, taking the outright lead at 15 under after two rounds. Jeeno Thitikul is second on 12 under.

England’s Charley Hull is among six players tied for third at 11 under after a bogey-free 67. The tournament’s $4m top prize is at stake on Sunday.

content.headline: Mudryk rejects Shevchenko’s account as dispute over drugs test escalates
content.shortHeadline: Mudryk rejects Shevchenko’s account of drugs-test dispute
content.standfirst: Mykhailo Mudryk says Andriy Shevchenko is lying about whether the winger asked a Ukrainian football official to take blame for his positive test. Mudryk repeats his allegations against the association and says he has evidence, which it has not yet responded to in the report.

image.caption: Mykhailo Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine.

sources.originalTitle: Shevchenko lying about drugs test claims - Mudryk

segments.body:
Mudryk has denied Shevchenko’s accusation that his representatives repeatedly asked a Ukrainian Association of Football employee to take the blame for his meldonium test. In a statement, the winger called that account a “lie” and said neither he nor his representatives made such a request.

Mudryk, who was suspended from November 2024 to July 2026, says he believes the substance entered his system while on international duty. He also accuses the association of withholding information and misleading his team, and says WhatsApp messages support his claim that he used its supplements at training camps.

content.headline: Ireland and South Africa meet amid suspensions and a charged build-up
content.shortHeadline: Ireland and South Africa meet amid disciplinary tensions
content.standfirst: South Africa face Ireland in Dublin without banned coach Rassie Erasmus, while both teams have had late changes to their squads. Ireland are looking to respond to a run of heavy defeats against leading sides.

image.caption: Siya Kolisi spoke about what rugby means to people in South Africa.

sources.originalTitle: 'No-one is going to break us' - defiant Boks face Ireland without Erasmus

segments.body:
Erasmus will miss the match after receiving a six-match ban for questioning officials following South Africa’s defeat by France. Assistant coach Mzwandile Stick backed him, while Ireland captain Dan Sheehan said the suspension had no effect on his team.

South Africa back-row Jasper Wiese is also suspended. Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast was cleared to play after being cited over an alleged hip-drop tackle.

segments.title: A test for Ireland
segments.body: Ireland have lost their past six matches against New Zealand, France and South Africa by double-digit margins. Sheehan, usually a hooker, will captain from number eight with several back-row players unavailable. South Africa have brought in Franco Mostert after Ruan Nortje was ruled out through injury.

perspectives.body: Stick says South Africa’s players remain united behind Erasmus. Ireland’s Sheehan, by contrast, said the disciplinary story has “zero impact” on his side’s preparation.

content.headline: Kulusevski and Everton captain Finnigan describe the toll of long injuries
content.shortHeadline: Kulusevski and Finnigan on the isolation of long injuries
content.standfirst: Dejan Kulusevski and Everton’s Megan Finnigan describe loneliness, doubts and the strain of lengthy rehabilitation. Both have returned to action after serious injuries kept them out for more than a season.

image.caption: Dejan Kulusevski has been working towards a return after a long injury absence.

sources.originalTitle: Loneliness & mood swings - what's it like to miss a season through injury?

segments.body: Tottenham’s Kulusevski says he wondered whether he could play again after a serious knee injury kept him out for 18 months and cost him a place at the 2026 World Cup. He returned as a substitute in October after 526 days away and says he no longer takes playing for granted.

segments.title: The mental toll
segments.body: Everton captain Finnigan says she lost her confidence and “sparkle” during 602 days out with a cruciate ligament injury. Former England midfielder Fara Williams also highlights the financial pressure some women face while injured, including bills and uncertainty over short-term contracts.

content.headline: Why Gen Z are falling for Jeff Buckley’s songs of yearning
content.shortHeadline: Gen Z find their yearning anthem in Jeff Buckley
content.standfirst: Streams, TikTok searches and a flourishing market for memorabilia point to a revival of Buckley’s music among young listeners. Fans describe its unguarded emotion as a contrast to online life and the difficulty of finding connection.

image.caption: Sydney Tripoli with memorabilia from her Jeff Buckley collection.

sources.originalTitle: Jeff Buckley was a 90s indie darling. Now gen Z think he’s the ‘yearner final boss’

segments.body: Nearly three decades after Jeff Buckley’s death at 30, young listeners are finding their way to his sole lifetime album, Grace. Fans interviewed for this report describe its mix of romance and despair as speaking to a generation drawn to the feeling of longing, even when real-world connection can seem hard to reach.

segments.title: A revival across platforms
segments.body: The report points to rising streams since 2022, more than 500,000 TikToks using “Lover, You Should Have Come Over” this year, and a recent increase in searches for Buckley. A documentary has also brought former partner Rebecca Moore’s account into wider view, presenting a more human portrait than the familiar mythology around the singer.

content.headline: Life Without Buildings return after a quarter-century away
content.shortHeadline: Life Without Buildings return after 25 years
content.standfirst: The Glasgow group’s unconventional music found a new audience through Frank Ocean and TikTok. Their reunion has brought back both the excitement of playing together and the fear of disturbing a once-cherished moment.

image.caption: Life Without Buildings around the release of their debut album.

sources.originalTitle: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?

segments.body: Life Without Buildings played together for only three years before splitting in 2002. Their album Any Other City was met with a hostile review at the time, but the band’s singular songs and Sue Tompkins’s rhythmic, carefully written vocals later found new listeners after Frank Ocean played “The Leanover” and Beabadoobee’s TikTok helped it travel further.

segments.title: Protecting the joy
segments.body: The four members had decided not to reunite, worried that returning might spoil what they remembered as a beautiful, self-contained chapter. A secret Glasgow show for charity shifted that feeling: the musicians found their old interlocking sound still alive, and Tompkins described feeling both afraid and energised by the performance.

content.headline: Kate Nash turns industry frustration into a new Irish-rooted album
content.shortHeadline: Kate Nash brings her Irish roots to a new album
content.standfirst: The singer’s forthcoming Cailín draws on Irish instruments and family history, while her campaigning continues to focus on the economics that make touring difficult for working musicians.

image.caption: Kate Nash.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business

segments.body: Kate Nash says she still needs unconventional ways to fund touring, despite earning from her catalogue. Her “Butts for Tour Buses” campaign used an OnlyFans account to help pay for a tour, and she argues that the industry’s economics threaten the mid-sized and smaller gigs that sustain musical culture.

segments.title: Making Cailín
segments.body: Her new album, recorded in Spiddal on Ireland’s west coast, explores her Irish heritage through uilleann pipes, flutes and tin whistle alongside punk and hip-hop. Nash says recording it helped her learn more about her family history, including her grandfather’s attempted journey to fight Franco’s forces in Spain.

content.headline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul find grief beneath the jokes
content.shortHeadline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul turn inward
content.standfirst: The Belgian duo’s next album keeps their playful art-pop but moves towards grief, family and parenthood. Their tour of Ghent and conversation about the record reveal the personal history behind its stranger images.

image.caption: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul in Ghent.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Would you breastfeed your own father?’ The goofy, spiky world of art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul

segments.body: After a debut that used wit and dance-pop to examine race, colonialism and online life, Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul say their next album, Mainland Madinina, is more introspective. They began writing in Martinique, where Adigéry’s family roots helped shape a record about growing older, raising children and processing loss.

segments.title: A new emotional register
segments.body: Adigéry’s father died between the two albums, and the new songs include “I’m Lost”, about finally throwing away flowers from his funeral. The duo say humour remains, but grief has changed the work: writing and performing the songs offered Adigéry a way to consider what family trauma is passed on and what might be left behind.

content.headline: Radie Peat’s solo debut lets her voice reshape traditional folk
content.shortHeadline: Radie Peat reshapes folk on her solo debut
content.standfirst: The Lankum singer’s first solo album moves through Irish, British and American song traditions, with inventive arrangements that keep her commanding voice at the centre.

sources.originalTitle: No Human Tongue Can Tell

segments.body: Radie Peat opens No Human Tongue Can Tell with a stark rendition of the traditional “Hares on the Mountain”. From there, the Lankum and ØXN singer makes her voice the record’s anchor, layering it across songs whose arrangements move between keyboards, concertina and more unexpected textures.

segments.title: Old songs, altered
segments.body: The album draws on songs from Irish, British and American traditions, often centring women with complicated lives. Its standout transformation, the review argues, is “The Moon and Stars”: a fiddle tune recast as a dense, trip-hop-leaning piece that builds to a crashing finish without losing the force of Peat’s singing.

content.headline: Thoom fuses hyperpop and Arabic sounds into an emotionally vivid debut
content.shortHeadline: Thoom makes hyperpop personal on a vivid debut
content.standfirst: On Everyday, Everything Is at Stake, the Beirut-born, Los Angeles-based artist joins hyperpop production with Arabic instrumentation and a forceful vocal performance, turning emotional conflict into music of scale.

sources.originalTitle: Everyday, Everything Is at Stake

segments.body: Zeynab Marwan, who records as Thoom, brings contrasting energies together on her debut mixtape: club music’s abrasive force, pop drama and Arabic instrumentation. Her voice is central, shifting from syrupy melody to a menacing edge as the production moves through oud, mizmar, drum machines and restless synths.

segments.title: Belonging and uncertainty
segments.body: The closing “I’m Going Back to Lebanon” holds two unresolved desires at once: to leave a lover and to return home. Its questions about whether the artist can go back connect the mixtape’s emotional intensity to Lebanon’s ongoing crisis, making the song, in the review’s view, its clearest expression of what the title puts at stake.

content.headline: Lorenzo Senni brings punk screams into his restless electronic world
content.shortHeadline: Lorenzo Senni collides punk with electronic music
content.standfirst: All Ages draws on the Milan producer’s teenage straight-edge punk years and his fascination with rave. Its collision of beatless synths and raw voices is often thrilling, even when the experiment falters.

image.caption: Lorenzo Senni.

sources.originalTitle: Trance, prog synths, guttural screaming: Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages is the year’s wildest electronic album

segments.body: Lorenzo Senni has built a career at a distance from the dancefloor, dissecting trance rather than simply making club music. On All Ages, he turns towards his own past as a straight-edge punk fan and sets guttural hardcore vocals against his familiar, beatless flurries of synths.

segments.title: When the voices take hold
segments.body: Samples from Refused’s Dennis Lyxzén and the late Tim Taylor, among others, give tracks such as “Self eXamined Endurance” a propulsive quality in place of a conventional beat. The review finds the mix of punk and electronics most persuasive there, while some choices, including the piano-and-strings “Purely Coincidental”, feel less connected to the album’s central idea.

content.headline: U2’s Carnaval De Luz finds renewed purpose in familiar sounds
content.shortHeadline: U2 reconnect with their strengths on Carnaval De Luz
content.standfirst: The band’s first new album since 2017 trades some of their more portentous habits for open-hearted songs. This review hears a strong return, while questioning whether it can restore their wider cultural standing.

sources.originalTitle: U2 lost the plot decades ago – their new album finally fixes that

segments.body: Carnaval De Luz revisits familiar U2 ingredients: soaring choruses, The Edge’s guitar and songs about community and hope. The review argues that a lighter touch gives the band’s first album since 2017 a renewed energy and makes it their strongest record in years.

segments.title: A comeback in a changed landscape
segments.body: The album’s self-references can feel deliberate, and not every song works; “The Mirror Maker (Rosalía)” is singled out as an awkward tribute. The review also cautions that a good record may not restore U2’s former dominance in a splintered music culture where rock no longer commands the same attention.

content.headline: You Can See Everything turns Elizabeth Holmes into a shifting target
content.shortHeadline: Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes film keeps shifting
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s film begins with access to Holmes before prison, then takes a startling turn. Its provocative use of reenactment leaves the viewer weighing performance against truth.

image.caption: Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: You Can See Everything review – unblinking, unhinged and unmissable

segments.body: Nathan Fielder spends time with Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before she went to prison, as she continues to insist that Theranos’s technology works. The review describes their conversations as a tense contest of polite faces, with Holmes’s certainty and evasions leaving Fielder—and the viewer—unsure how much she believes her own claims.

segments.title: Reenactment as a provocation
segments.body: After Holmes is sent to prison, Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim bring in Amanda Seyfried, who played Holmes in The Dropout, to recreate conversations they could not film. The device shifts the film’s focus from what Holmes may be concealing to the roles people perform, while leaving open how much of the story’s mystery has been shaped by editing.

content.headline: Josephine confronts sexual violence through a child’s perspective
content.shortHeadline: Josephine explores a child’s trauma after witnessing rape
content.standfirst: Beth de Araújo’s film follows an eight-year-old who witnesses a rape and struggles to understand what she saw. Its approach is grounded in the director’s experience, though one review finds some of its choices contrived.

image.caption: Channing Tatum and Mason Reeves in Josephine.

sources.originalTitle: 'The subject is still taboo': Shocking new film Josephine confronts sexual violence through a child's eyes
Josephine review – Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan ballast knotty drama about a child witness to a rape

segments.body: In Josephine, an eight-year-old girl witnesses a rape in a San Francisco park. Director Beth de Araújo says the story draws on her own childhood experience and asks viewers to imagine a child learning what sexual violence is through a moment she cannot yet process. The film also follows the effects on Josephine’s parents, played by Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan.

segments.title: A difficult question of representation
segments.body: De Araújo and film scholar Tanya Horeck discuss the ethics of showing sexual violence on screen, including what a rape scene is doing and whose perspective it serves. The Guardian review praises young lead Mason Reeves but finds the film’s recurring image of the attacker and parts of its courtroom plot contrived, underlining that the film’s bold subject does not remove questions about execution.

perspectives.body: The Guardian review calls Reeves outstanding but argues that the film’s repeated use of the attacker as a silent presence becomes contrived, and that its courtroom ending leaves an important real-world question unresolved.

content.headline: Anthony Boyle moves between a struggling courier and a crypto founder
content.shortHeadline: Anthony Boyle on playing a courier and Sam Bankman-Fried
content.standfirst: The Belfast-born actor discusses I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, about precarious work, and his role as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists. He says the characters have left him thinking about the distance between money and power.

image.caption: Anthony Boyle.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Sam-Bankman Fried messaged me from prison’: rising star Anthony Boyle on playing the disgraced tech bro – and a zero-hours bike courier

segments.body: Anthony Boyle plays Patrick, a politically outspoken bike courier supporting a young family on zero-hours work, in I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning. Boyle says the character’s struggle to get by should remind audiences that people live on precarious wages, adding that he hopes viewers might think about tipping a delivery worker.

segments.title: A very different kind of role
segments.body: Boyle also plays FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists. He says he exchanged more than 100 questions with Bankman-Fried through a prison messaging service, though he promised not to reveal what they discussed. Boyle draws a contrast between Patrick’s financial insecurity and the wealth associated with Bankman-Fried, saying his own focus is on doing good work rather than money.

content.headline: Wicker’s strange romance turns domestic expectations upside down
content.shortHeadline: Wicker makes a strange, funny case for equal partnership
content.standfirst: A woman commissions a husband made of willow in a bawdy, deliberately odd fairy tale. The film’s creators and commentators connect its appeal to domestic labour and desire; one critic finds its gender politics troubling but funny.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker
Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, Olivia Colman plays an ostracised fisherwoman who commissions a basketmaker to make her a husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård. The filmmakers say the premise grew into a story about domestic labour, dating and the pressures women face in relationships, even as its fairy-tale village and sex comedy keep the tone deliberately strange.

segments.title: Fantasy, agency and laughter
segments.body: Commentators place the film in a tradition of romances between humans and monsters, where desire and difference can unsettle social expectations. The i Paper review calls the story sexist in its depiction of the husband’s lack of agency, but says Colman’s character’s relief at having a kind, supportive partner gives the fantasy its appeal.

perspectives.body: The i Paper reviewer finds Wicker’s husband troublingly without agency, yet enjoys the film’s bawdy comedy and its fantasy of a man who supports his wife without expecting subordination in return.

content.headline: Alex Cox on independent film, Bond and the chaos of Sid and Nancy
content.shortHeadline: Alex Cox on Sid and Nancy, Bond and indie filmmaking
content.standfirst: The director revisits his cult films, explains why he is crowdfunding Repo Man 2 and offers blunt views on franchises. He also recalls John Lydon’s furious response to Sid and Nancy.

image.caption: Alex Cox.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Cox: ‘John Lydon said Sid and Nancy was a nightmarish piece of garbage’

segments.body: In a question-and-answer interview, Alex Cox recalls that John Lydon called the Sid and Nancy script a “nightmarish piece of garbage”. Cox says Lydon also advised him to fictionalise the story further, and that the resulting controversy proved useful when the film came out.

segments.title: Keeping films independent
segments.body: Cox is crowdfunding Repo Man 2, set in a world of driverless cars. He argues that independent filmmakers have reason to seek support directly from audiences, saying studios and large streamers are more interested in franchises and intellectual property than in scripts. He also gives an unsparing assessment of contemporary franchise filmmaking.

content.headline: Guarding Stars makes holiday-romance silliness work
content.shortHeadline: Leighton Meester shines in Guarding Stars
content.standfirst: Leighton Meester brings wit and warmth to a familiar Christmas romcom formula about a bodyguard and a movie star. The review finds the film’s silliness part of its appeal.

image.caption: Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki in Guarding Stars.

sources.originalTitle: Guarding Stars review – Leighton Meester is a delight in fizzy Netflix holiday romance

segments.body: Leighton Meester plays a no-nonsense bodyguard assigned to protect a film star at his family’s Montana ranch. The setup is far-fetched, the review concedes, but Meester’s sharp performance gives Hannah enough personality to make the predictable holiday-romance beats enjoyable.

The film follows familiar seasonal conventions—an awkward fake relationship, a family gathering and a late romantic turn—but adds brisk action and a warm supporting cast. The review says Meester’s performance makes the combination of female competence and Christmas sentiment work better than expected.

content.headline: The Altruists makes a chaotic crypto scandal compelling television
content.shortHeadline: The Altruists turns the FTX scandal into tense TV
content.standfirst: Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play Caroline Ellison and Sam Bankman-Fried in a fast-moving account of FTX’s rise and collapse. The review praises the performances while warning that the financial detail can be hard to follow.

image.caption: Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

sources.originalTitle: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale

segments.body: The Altruists traces the relationship between Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison from their early work together to FTX’s collapse. The series links their commitment to effective altruism with the self-image and rationalisations that surround their decisions, as the company’s apparent idealism gives way to fraud and financial ruin.

segments.title: A high-wire performance
segments.body: The Guardian review praises Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner, and says their performances keep the series just coherent enough to follow. It finds some of the financial mechanics difficult to grasp, but sees the show’s larger subject as the danger of concentrating wealth and power in people who believe they are acting for the greater good.

content.headline: I Am Helen puts the women harmed by toxic masculinity in focus
content.shortHeadline: I Am Helen centres women’s experience of toxic masculinity
content.standfirst: Nicola Coughlan plays a woman whose partner’s misogynistic ideas turn into coercion and violence. The review argues that the drama’s unsettling force lies in showing how ordinary the behaviour can appear.

image.caption: Nicola Coughlan as Helen and Joe Cole as Steve in I Am Helen.

sources.originalTitle: All men should watch I Am Helen

segments.body: The latest instalment of Dominic Savage’s anthology follows Helen, played by Nicola Coughlan, as her partner Steve’s seemingly ordinary grievances harden into controlling behaviour. A non-consensual act of violence is followed by him casting himself as the victim, and Helen is left apologising as their life appears to return to normal.

segments.title: The ordinary roots of harm
segments.body: The review argues that the drama’s most disturbing scenes show misogyny seeping into daily life: a colleague’s advice and familiar claims of male victimhood help Steve justify his expectations of women. It says the story shifts attention from destructive men to the women who bear the consequences.

content.headline: The Last Spy finds a complicated history behind a CIA career
content.shortHeadline: The Last Spy follows Peter Sichel through cold war history
content.standfirst: A long interview with refugee-turned-CIA officer Peter Sichel gives this documentary an extraordinary central voice. The review also notes what remains unknowable about his work and the people he recruited.

image.caption: Peter Sichel in The Last Spy.

sources.originalTitle: The Last Spy review – a riveting tale of CIA meddling, espionage gossip and Blue Nun wine

segments.body: Peter Sichel recounts fleeing Germany with his family, joining the US army and becoming a German-speaking intelligence officer. The documentary follows his career through the emergence of the CIA and the cold war, while Sichel’s dry, candid account keeps the history rooted in one life.

segments.title: The secrets left untold
segments.body: The Guardian review finds Sichel’s changing views on communism and US power more revealing than a conventional spy adventure. But he keeps quiet about what he and his agents did, leaving the documentary with an unresolved gap between the historical importance of his work and the details he will disclose.

content.headline: Heated Rivalry’s 4DX screenings turn romance into a physical gag
content.shortHeadline: Heated Rivalry fans test its 4DX thrills
content.standfirst: Fans in hockey jerseys watched episodes of the romance in seats that moved, vibrated and sprayed water. The experience was often ridiculous and funny, though one viewer said the effects could undercut the emotion.

image.caption: Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams in Heated Rivalry.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I hope paramedics are on standby for the sex scenes!’ The wet and wild TV experience leaving fans dizzy

segments.body: Cineworld’s 4DX screenings of Heated Rivalry paired episodes of the queer hockey romance with moving seats, water, wind and other sensory effects. Fans interviewed at the event arrived curious about how the technology would handle the show’s hockey scenes, text messages and intimate moments.

segments.title: A very silly spectacle
segments.body: The crowd laughed as seat vibrations accompanied messages and the audience was splashed during a scene by a lake. Some movement worked better than others, and one fan said the effects could distract from the emotional story. For many in the room, though, the absurdity was precisely the appeal.

content.headline: December’s TV highlights include new Austen and Harry Potter adaptations
content.shortHeadline: What to watch on TV this December
content.standfirst: A BBC guide to the month’s new series ranges from Pride and Prejudice and Harry Potter to returning comedies and crime dramas, with international streaming dates included.

sources.originalTitle: Harry Potter to Pride and Prejudice: 10 of the best TV shows to watch this December

segments.body: The December selection includes new adaptations of Pride and Prejudice and Harry Potter, alongside a return for Only Murders in the Building and a holiday special for The Other Bennet Sister. The guide gives cast details and describes how each production approaches familiar stories and characters.

segments.title: More to stream
segments.body: The list also covers a submarine thriller, a JonBenét Ramsey drama, a story of the Indian diaspora in the US, and returning shows including Emily in Paris. Each entry includes premiere information for the services and regions supplied in the guide.

content.headline: Why Grand Theft Auto is unlikely to become a TV series
content.shortHeadline: Why Grand Theft Auto may never work as a TV series
content.standfirst: Take-Two says an adaptation would need to delight players, but this essay argues that GTA’s open-ended play is the very thing a scripted series would struggle to preserve.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto would be a huge TV series – here’s why it will never happen

segments.body: Take-Two chief executive Strauss Zelnick says a film or television adaptation of Grand Theft Auto is not ruled out, but would need to engage and delight players. The Guardian essay argues that the game’s appeal comes from the freedom for different players to have radically different experiences—something a single scripted narrative would flatten.

segments.title: Some worlds resist adaptation
segments.body: The piece compares GTA with works such as Maus and Calvin and Hobbes, whose creators have argued that their original forms serve them best. It also notes that those refusals may not last forever, pointing to One Hundred Years of Solitude, which reached television after its author had died.

content.headline: GTA VI tips for players—and why its 18 rating matters
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI: practical tips and a warning for parents
content.standfirst: A guide to avoiding trouble in Leonida offers advice on cash, heat and heists, while a separate report details the game’s explicit sex, drugs and violence. Both make clear that the sprawling new world is made for adults.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI, an adults-only game.

sources.originalTitle: Bank your stolen cash, bring a change of clothes, go easy on the bloodshed: 15 tips for playing Grand Theft Auto VI
‘Definitely one of the best games I’ve ever played’: our games editor answered your GTA VI questions
Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child

segments.title: Getting around Leonida
segments.body: The Guardian’s guide recommends banking cash at ATMs, using a getaway car rather than your own for crimes, and changing clothes or vehicles to reduce police attention. It also advises players to use checkpoint retries during missions, avoid unnecessary violence and take their time with the large game.

segments.title: An adults-only world
segments.body: A separate report warns parents that GTA VI’s 18 rating reflects far more than violence: it describes explicit sex, full-frontal nudity, drugs and vulgar dialogue. The games editor similarly tells parents to consider the material and their teenager’s exposure before deciding whether the game is appropriate.

content.headline: The Wii and PlayStation 3 imagined gaming’s future in different ways
content.shortHeadline: The Wii and PS3 offered rival visions of gaming
content.standfirst: Twenty years on, the Wii’s accessible motion controls and the PS3’s technical ambition both look influential—and incomplete. This retrospective traces what each console got right and where its vision fell short.

image.caption: Nintendo’s Wii and Sony’s PlayStation 3.

sources.originalTitle: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?

segments.body: Nintendo’s Wii made motion controls and accessible play its pitch, with Wii Sports turning the console into a fixture of family gatherings. Sony’s PlayStation 3 promised technical power, online connectivity and long, ambitious games, while also supporting independent developers.

segments.title: Two legacies
segments.body: The retrospective argues that neither company’s vision fully won: gaming now includes both intuitive, accessible experiences and enormous, demanding adventures. The Wii sold more consoles, while the PS3 helped set foundations for online play and technically ambitious games; each also left parts of its promise unrealised.

content.headline: Can an Elden Ring film make its bleak fantasy world matter?
content.shortHeadline: The challenge facing an Elden Ring film
content.standfirst: Alex Garland’s adaptation has a major game, a prominent mythology and a reported large budget behind it. The challenge, this essay argues, is making audiences care about the world rather than merely explaining it.

image.caption: Elden Ring, the game being adapted for film.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: The forthcoming Elden Ring adaptation is written and directed by Alex Garland and has a cast that includes Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw, Nick Offerman and Jonathan Pryce. The game has sold more than 30 million copies, but its vast world and grim, often horrific imagery make the move to film a difficult one.

segments.title: World-building is not enough
segments.body: The essay compares the project with fantasy adaptations that struggled to turn elaborate source material into compelling cinema. Garland’s films have resisted conventional reassurance, but the piece raises the question of whether that approach can survive the reported scale of this production—and what kind of story could give viewers a reason to stay in the Lands Between.

content.headline: Colibactin toxin emerges as a leading suspect in early-onset bowel cancer
content.shortHeadline: A gut toxin is a leading suspect in bowel cancer under 50
content.standfirst: Researchers told MPs that early exposure to colibactin, produced by some E coli, may help explain rising bowel cancer rates in younger people. Its role remains under investigation.

image.caption: E coli bacteria in the gut; some variants produce the toxin colibactin, a suspected contributor to early-onset bowel cancer.

sources.originalTitle: Bacterial toxin produced by E coli leading suspect in rise in bowel cancer among under-50s

segments.body: Bowel cancer cases among people under 50 have doubled in many countries over the past two decades. Known risks such as obesity, smoking and alcohol explain only about half of cases, researchers told a parliamentary committee, prompting a search for other causes.

segments.title: A clue, not a conclusion
segments.body: Colibactin, a toxin made by some E coli in the gut, is a leading suspect. Mutations associated with the toxin were three times more common in tumours from people under 40 than in those over 70. Scientists are investigating whether it drives cancer; they have not established that it does. Evidence of mutations in some children raises the possibility that exposure early in life could matter.

Researchers also said that established risks remain important. Cancer epidemiologist Elio Riboli told MPs that applying what is already known about prevention could avert many cancers, even as scientists work to identify other causes.

content.headline: Dispute over IPCC report timing puts climate science and global stocktake at a ‘
content.shortHeadline: IPCC report delay risks disrupting climate negotiations
content.standfirst: Some countries want to delay the next major climate assessment until after a 2028 review of Paris pledges. Scientists and negotiators warn that slowing the work could complicate cooperation and weaken the process.

sources.originalTitle: IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist

segments.body: The next comprehensive assessment by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change is under way, with completion hoped for in 2028. Its findings are expected to inform that year’s global stocktake of progress under the Paris agreement, which will assess whether countries’ emissions pledges are sufficient.

segments.title: A contested timetable
segments.body: Russia, India and the Arab group, including Saudi Arabia, have argued for publication in 2029, after the stocktake. They say developing countries are disadvantaged in the process, and some critics describe the IPCC’s mitigation scenarios as biased against the global south. Climate scientist Johan Rockström rejects that charge and says the pathways reflect peer-reviewed evidence.

The IPCC says 51% of the 664 appointed report authors come from developing countries and economies in transition. Some developing countries, including small island states and least developed countries, want the report completed without delay. The IPCC’s budget is also under discussion; without an agreement, producing the assessment in time for the stocktake could become harder.

content.headline: Small keto study for anorexia prompts questions about evidence and private money
content.shortHeadline: Anorexia keto study raises questions about evidence and funding
content.standfirst: A small trial found symptom improvements for some participants, but it cannot establish that a restrictive diet treats anorexia. The investigation also examines how a wealthy family’s funding may shape the research agenda.

sources.originalTitle: Roblox money is pushing a controversial anorexia treatment

segments.body: A 14-week study explored whether a ketogenic diet was safe and feasible for people with anorexia; it was not designed to prove the diet works. Of 22 people recruited, 18 completed the trial. Twelve no longer met the study’s diagnostic criteria for anorexia at the end, and the lead researcher said none lost weight. The trial did not compare the diet with standard treatment.

segments.title: Caution about a restrictive diet
segments.body: Psychiatrists and nutrition experts interviewed by The Verge warned that the findings are too limited to support claims of effectiveness. They note that restricting food may be risky for people with eating disorders, and that some participants’ symptoms worsened. Researchers say larger, controlled trials are needed; experts also stress that the study does not justify replacing established care.

segments.title: Who sets the research agenda?
segments.body: The report traces substantial private funding from the Baszucki family for ketogenic-diet research and raises questions about how philanthropic priorities can steer a field, especially as public research funding falls. The family’s spokesperson said its focus is on interventions that government and industry have been slow to support; the reporting also details disagreements about how the evidence and one patient’s treatment story were presented.

content.headline: NHS hospitals prepare to offer Alzheimer’s blood tests before trials report
content.shortHeadline: Some NHS hospitals plan Alzheimer’s blood tests before trial results
content.standfirst: Blood tests may speed up assessment for people with memory problems, but access is likely to vary. Two large trials are still under way, and the tests should be used as part of clinical assessment rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis.

sources.originalTitle: The simple test that will diagnose Alzheimer’s within days – available next year

segments.body: Some UK hospitals plan to introduce blood tests for Alzheimer’s in memory clinics and neurology departments, potentially shortening a diagnosis that can take months or years. University College Hospital in London is already offering the test, and Manchester Brain Health Centre says it expects to start within weeks.

segments.title: Access and limits
segments.body: The test measures a form of tau protein, which can help clinicians assess whether Alzheimer’s is likely and distinguish it from some other causes of memory problems. Two large trials examining how the tests fit into NHS services are due to finish in 2029. There is no central list of hospitals offering the service, raising the possibility of uneven access.

Doctors say results need to be interpreted alongside clinical and cognitive assessments. Private testing outside a memory clinic could produce false positives, while a blood test may help rule out Alzheimer’s when symptoms have another cause. Faster identification could support care planning and help some people access trials or treatment options.

content.headline: Wreck of Australia’s first locally built warship found 128 years after sinking
content.shortHeadline: Australia’s first locally built warship found after 128 years
content.standfirst: Marine archaeologists found the wooden gunboat Spitfire off Queensland on the anniversary of its 1898 sinking. The wreck is protected, adding a newly located vessel to Australia’s maritime heritage.

image.caption: Illustration of the HMCS Spitfire, Australia’s first locally built warship.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Remarkable luck’: wreck of first Australian-built warship discovered exactly 128 years after sinking

segments.body: The wreck of the 19-metre Spitfire was found off far north Queensland on 21 August, exactly 128 years after it sank. A team from the Australian National Maritime Museum, Queensland government and Royal Australian Navy located it using sonar during a month-long search guided by archival records.

segments.title: A vessel with changing roles
segments.body: Built in Sydney in 1855, the gunboat was commissioned by the colonial government amid concern about Russian and French military presence in the region. It later served Queensland as a pilot vessel before being sold for use in sea-cucumber fishing. The crew were rescued when it foundered in 1898.

content.headline: UK tribunal orders government to confirm secret Apple encryption order
content.shortHeadline: UK government ordered to confirm secret Apple data order
content.standfirst: A tribunal has rejected the Home Office’s claim that confirming the order would harm national security. The government has yet to confirm it, and a further hearing is expected to consider what details can be made public.
